findings.claim: a strategic-org-design framework whose worked examples and framework mappings are predominantly drawn from software organisations
findings.failure_mode: Overstates the software share. Most of the Primer's named examples are non-software (costume department, surgical team, special forces, sous-chef, insurance claims, movie producer, diner, Haier), and the 2025 Edition explicitly broadens applicability to service organisations.
findings.evidence: Deep 253-268 (named-case list); deep 290 (p. 4): 'broaden applicability from product development to service organizations'. Converted source 18-20 (p. 1): 'OT applies to Farms and Pharma. Software and Services. Consulting and Construction.'
findings.fix: correct: a strategic-org-design framework with several software worked examples (the Software Feature Team, the running MADE example, the pet-supply e-commerce example, the SAFe mapping) alongside non-software ones

findings.claim: SAFe, LeSS, and Team Topologies are mapped to OT topology regions.
findings.failure_mode: Only SAFe (and RDHY) are mapped in the Primer. LeSS and Team Topologies are listed among 'more framework mappings examples' with a pointer to the website; no mapping is given.
findings.evidence: Deep 191-194 (p. 22): list of frameworks 'that can be mapped onto the OT grid'; two mappings illustrated (SAFe, RDHY). Converted source 1321-1330: 'More framework mappings examples: ... Learn more: orgtopologies.com/framework-mapping'.
findings.fix: correct: SAFe is mapped onto the OT grid; LeSS, Team Topologies and others are listed as mappable, with the mappings held on the OT website.

findings.claim: *"no guarantee... that the output effectively solves the real problem or creates outcomes people care about. Products and services with 'feature bloat' are a common consequence."*
findings.failure_mode: Verbatim deep-ref [V] passage carried without its marker.
findings.evidence: Deep 102 and 219 (p. 12, "Delivery Topology") [V].
findings.fix: re-mark: [V]

findings.claim: a counter to the most common software-business failure: choosing an engineering framework (SAFe, LeSS, Scrum-at-scale variants) as the business strategy
findings.failure_mode: Frequency claim ('most common') not in the source. The Primer calls framework thinking the consulting pitch and the easy path of following the crowd, without ranking it.
findings.evidence: Deep 181 (p. 22): 'This is the pitch from consulting companies big and small, and naturally, it seems easier to follow the crowd'.
findings.fix: correct: a counter to a familiar software-business failure, which the Primer calls 'the pitch from consulting companies big and small': choosing an engineering framework as the business strategy

findings.claim: The pet-supply worked example walks an AI build-vs-buy-vs-integrate decision at the architecture-team-cost-customer intersection.
findings.failure_mode: Attributes to the Primer's example a build/buy/integrate and architecture decision it does not contain. The example walks where to focus AI investment, the dominant constraint, and human monitoring.
findings.evidence: Deep 170 (p. 21) and converted source 1199-1219: objective, org goal, target (Delivery, CAPS-3), focus departments, front-end skills bottleneck, AI agents that design and code front ends, monitoring by existing specialists. No build/buy/integrate or architecture content.
findings.fix: correct: The pet-supply worked example walks the three questions end to end: where to focus AI investment, which constraint AI should target, and who monitors the agents.

findings.claim: Rendanheyi as elevating thousands of MEs to Driving archetypes
findings.failure_mode: Adds a map placement ('to Driving archetypes') that neither the deep ref nor the source text states.
findings.evidence: Deep 194 (p. 22): 'The OT map demonstrates how RDHY elevates its thousands of micro-enterprises (MEs) that directly interact with users'.
findings.fix: correct: Rendanheyi as elevating thousands of micro-enterprises that interact directly with users

findings.claim: Rendanheyi is a software-business reference for what an Adaptive-Topology-at-scale looks like
findings.failure_mode: The Primer does not call RDHY an Adaptive Topology, and Haier is not a software business; the Primer calls RDHY 'an innovative management philosophy'.
findings.evidence: Deep 194 (p. 22): RDHY 'an innovative management philosophy ... aiming to align every employee's efforts directly with customer (or user) value creation'; 'elevates its thousands of micro-enterprises'.
findings.fix: correct: Rendanheyi is the Primer's example of an organisation elevating thousands of user-facing units at scale, useful when senior leadership asks "can we get there from here".

findings.claim: bottleneck is front-end skill; AI investment targeted at front-end agents ... This is the canonical worked example for a software business deciding *which* AI capability to build/buy/integrate.
findings.failure_mode: The bottleneck and targeting steps are in the converted source but not in the deep reference; 'build/buy/integrate' is not in the example (see D005).
findings.evidence: Converted source 1208-1213 (p. 21): 'a lack of front-end design and coding skilled people. Focus time, money, and management attention on AIs, especially on that big bottleneck'. Deep 170 omits these steps.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add source 1205-1213 (the three question-answers) to deep 170 as [V] (p. 21); correct: This is the Primer's worked example for a software business deciding *where* to aim AI investment.

findings.claim: SAFe lands mostly at TASKS and CAPS; LeSS lands at CAPS-3 / PART-2; FAST Agile lands at Adaptive; Spotify model varies.
findings.failure_mode: Only the SAFe placement is in the Primer. The LeSS, FAST Agile and Spotify placements are stated as fact with no source.
findings.evidence: Deep 191-193 (p. 22): SAFe mapping given; LeSS, FAST Agile, Spotify only listed as frameworks 'that can be mapped'. Converted source 1321-1334: list plus website pointer.
findings.fix: correct: Given the target topology, which framework's practices help us elevate? The Primer maps SAFe mostly to TASKS and CAPS (p. 22); map any other candidate the same way before choosing. The framework is the means, not the end.

findings.claim: The OT mapping is essentially a Conway's-Law analysis: the software architecture will reflect the team boundaries.
findings.failure_mode: Characterises OT mapping as a Conway's-Law analysis. Conway's Law appears nowhere in the Primer, its deep ref, or the Letaw deep ref; OT maps units by skills and work mandate.
findings.evidence: No 'Conway' in deep 1-299, converted source 1-1582, or letaw-handbook-sweng-methods-deep (grep). Deep 128 (p. 16): MAP = map units on archetypes, their inputs, outputs and dependencies.
findings.fix: strip

findings.section: Questions, Phase 3, 'Test the PMO / Resource-Topology drift'
findings.claim: "The Directing Archetypes in the upper left quadrant treat the Doing Archetypes as 'resources,'" — this is the named drift pattern.
findings.failure_mode: The Primer names no drift pattern; the quoted sentence describes how the Resource Topology works, not a drift. The quote is re-extracted from the source (not in the deep) and unmarked. The PMO link itself is supported (p. 14).
findings.evidence: Converted source 618-619 (p. 11) holds the sentence; deep 100 omits it. Deep 112 (p. 14): Resource use case 'PMO resource management of specialists'. No drift content in deep 1-299.
findings.fix: correct: As the company grows, does the PMO function reassert Resource-Topology framing? The Primer's Resource Topology is the 'PMO resource management of specialists' case (p. 14). cycle-to-deep: add the p. 11 'Directing Archetypes ... matching skill demand with skill supply' sentence to deep 100 as [V]

findings.section: Questions, Phase 5, 'Acknowledge the topology's named failure mode'
findings.claim: (Resource: coordination; Delivery: feature bloat; Adaptive: high-variance outcomes)
findings.failure_mode: The Primer names no failure mode for the Adaptive Topology; 'high-variance outcomes' recasts its stated use case ('fast delivery of uncertain results') as a failure.
findings.fix: correct: (Resource: coordination; Delivery: feature bloat; Adaptive: no failure mode named by the Primer)

findings.claim: AI-driven elevation often surfaces coordination and prioritisation bottlenecks.
findings.failure_mode: Empirical generalisation not in the source. The Primer's stated new consequence of AI is human monitoring responsibility.
findings.evidence: Deep 160-168 (p. 20): expertise vanishing; bottleneck targeting; 'monitoring will become an important responsibility for human workers'. No coordination or prioritisation claim.
findings.fix: strip: second sentence

findings.claim: forcing one design on all is named as a missed-fit pattern. (p. 18)
findings.failure_mode: The Primer permits different designs for different parts of the company; it does not name single-design as a pattern.
findings.evidence: Deep 146 (p. 18): 'Companies may also choose different org designs for different parts of the company'.
findings.fix: correct: forcing one design on all ignores the Primer's point that different parts of a company may need their own goal and design. (p. 18)

findings.claim: Common in publicly-traded software businesses where utilisation reporting reasserts Resource-Topology framing. The named drift pattern that must be defended against. (p. 11)
findings.failure_mode: Neither the frequency claim nor the 'named drift pattern' is in the Primer, and the p. 11 citation carries no such content.
findings.evidence: Deep 100 (p. 11): Resource Topology description and fit; no drift, public-company or utilisation-reporting content anywhere in deep 1-299.
findings.fix: correct: **Drift back to Resource Topology under quarterly-predictability pressure.** Utilisation reporting can pull an elevated organisation back toward Resource-Topology framing; periodic re-mapping (p. 19) is how to see it.

findings.claim: AI investment focus: R&D (the elevation area). Bottleneck: front-end design and coding skill.
findings.failure_mode: These steps are in the converted source but not the deep reference; the source names Product Management and R&D as the focus, not R&D alone.
findings.evidence: Converted source 1205-1211 (p. 21): 'The Product Management and R&D departments, so focus on AI investment there.' ... 'a lack of front-end design and coding skilled people'. Deep 170 omits both.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: same passage as D008; correct: AI investment focus: Product Management and R&D

findings.claim: A reference for what Adaptive-at-scale looks like in practice
findings.failure_mode: The Primer does not classify RDHY as an Adaptive Topology; it says the map shows RDHY elevating its micro-enterprises.
findings.fix: correct: A reference for elevation at scale in practice

findings.claim: A software-business reference for divergent-design accommodation: same company, different product lines, different topologies.
findings.failure_mode: Re-purposes the Primer's Partial-Business example. The Primer uses Uber Ride vs Uber Eats to illustrate a vertical level (separate profit centres), and elsewhere as scopes for an Adaptive Team-of-Teams; it never says the two hold different topologies.
findings.evidence: Deep 47 (p. 7): 'two separate profit centers within a single company' as Partial-Business Focus. Deep 104 (p. 13): Adaptive Team-of-Teams 'across the entire business ("Uber") or a partial business domain ("Uber Eats")'.
findings.fix: correct: Two separate profit centres within one company, each a Partial-Business unit with cross-team collaboration inside it (p. 7). Pair it with the p. 18 point that divisions may carry their own goal and design.

findings.claim: Designed target: Delivery Topology with cross-functional end-to-end teams. Elevated: Doing archetypes restructured into two cross-functional end-to-end teams.
findings.failure_mode: Supported by the converted source but absent from the deep reference, which stops the running example at ASSESS.
findings.evidence: Converted source 1068-1069 (p. 18) and 1146-1149 (p. 19). Deep 140-154 carry neither sentence.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add "If flow is the goal, the Delivery Topology becomes a suitable choice." [V] (p. 18) and "In the example mapping on the right, the separate Doing Archetypes have been restructured into two cross-functional, end-to-end teams, elevating the organization from the Resource to the Delivery Topology." [V] (p. 19)

findings.claim: Jones provides the empirical software-economics base (intangible-product pricing, AI-integration cost modelling, agency-theory analysis, Bass diffusion) ... Where OT names the topology choice, Jones prices it.
findings.failure_mode: Jones's deep ref has intangible products, pricing, agency theory and Bass diffusion, but no AI-integration cost modelling; and Jones does not price topology choices.
findings.evidence: jones-evidence-based-sweng-deep 85-87 (intangible goods), 99 (agency theory, Ch 3.4.6-3.4.7), 101-103 (pricing, Bass diffusion). No AI content (grep for AI/artificial finds none relevant).
findings.fix: correct: Jones provides the empirical software-economics base (intangible-product economics, pricing, agency-theory analysis, Bass diffusion) that complements OT's strategic-design framework.

findings.claim: Conway's Law connects them: the architecture choice and the topology choice are two views of the same decision.
findings.failure_mode: Conway's Law is in neither the Letaw deep ref nor the Primer; the bridge is invented.
findings.evidence: No 'Conway' in letaw-handbook-sweng-methods-deep, org-topologies-primer-2025-deep, or the converted Primer (grep).
findings.fix: strip: the Conway's Law sentence

notes: Structure deviates from the projection template: no 'What to Look For' or 'When to Use This Reference' sections; renamed Anti-Patterns and Worked Examples headings; no blockquoted [V] passages; Citation notes lack borrowed-through gaps and evidence-marker continuity. Inline [V] quotations all match the deep ref and converted source (DoD mapping, transaction/switching costs, Resource learning, Feature Factory, Adaptive merge, synchronicity, chain-of-fit passage, SAFe mapping, RDHY fragment, AI insight and three questions, divergent designs, output/outcome, CAPS-2 ecosystem sentence, incremental elevation, single-team, local optimisation); several truncate a sentence and close with a period without an ellipsis. The file's strongest drift is toward software-industry colour the Primer does not supply (Conway's Law, LeSS/FAST/Spotify placements, build-vs-buy).
